intro.title: Saying no without a quarrel
paragraphs: A colleague asks you to cover their shift on Saturday — your only day off in two weeks. You want both to help and to rest.
Choose what to say. If an answer doesn’t work, you stay where you are, see the reaction and understand why.
intro.note: The other person’s styles are patterns of behaviour, not types of people: the same person acts differently on different days. Real people react differently, so this is practice with wording, not a prediction.
intro.disclaimer: A learning simulation. The material draws on well-known communication methods (sources are given at each step), but it has not yet been reviewed by a psychologist.

variants.name: Pushy
variants.desc: Speaks briefly, presses and rushes you.

variants.name: Plays on your pity
variants.desc: Asks gently, complains and expects you “won’t let them down”.

nodes.narr: Lunch at a café near the office. Your colleague sits down opposite and gets straight to the point: they need someone to cover their shift on Saturday. Saturday is your only day off in two weeks.

options.text: OK, I’ll do it.
options.why: Agreeing “on autopilot”, out of awkwardness or guilt, usually turns into tiredness and resentment. You haven’t decided yet, and you’ve already given away your day off.

direct.say: Great! I knew I could count on you.

evasive.say: Oh, thank you, thank you! I knew you wouldn’t say no.

options.text: Give me a minute to think. I’ll tell you as soon as I decide.
options.why: You don’t have to answer instantly. A short pause protects you from agreeing under pressure and gives you time to put together a calm answer.

direct.say: Go on then, just be quick.

evasive.say: OK… it’s just that I really need to know.

options.text: No! How can you even ask that?
options.why: A sharp refusal with a reproach turns a request into a quarrel. You can say no calmly, without attacking.

direct.say: Hey, easy. I was just asking.

evasive.say: Why like that… I asked nicely.

options.text: My grandma is ill, I’m visiting her on Saturday.
options.why: A made-up reason is easy to check, and next time you’ll have to invent a new one. Saying no doesn’t need a “good excuse”.

direct.say: Ah, OK then… Although people are usually free at weekends.

evasive.say: Oh, what a shame… maybe the evening would work?

options.text: Well… I don’t know… maybe…
options.why: A vague answer keeps hope alive and drags out the pressure: the other person will come back again and again.

direct.say: So yes or no? I need to know.

evasive.say: So, maybe? I’ll wait for now.

tech.name: A pause before answering
tech.src: Ury, «The Power of a Positive No», 2007
tech.text: Don’t answer a request right away under pressure: take a minute to understand what you actually want.

nodes.hint: You don’t have to answer immediately. What can you say to buy time?

direct.say: Cover my Saturday shift, would you? Your Saturday’s free anyway.

evasive.say: Oh, I’m in such trouble… I have a shift on Saturday and I just can’t. Will you help me out? There’s no one else to ask.

nodes.narr: A minute has passed. Decision made: you’re not working on Saturday.

options.text: Thanks for trusting me, but I can’t do Saturday.
options.why: This is “yes” to the relationship and “no” to the request: you thank them and state the decision briefly, without excuses or blame.

direct.say: You can’t… OK. But that’s unpleasant.

evasive.say: You can’t… oh. I understand.

options.text: You see, I have only one day off, I need rest, there’s the renovation, then relatives are coming, and anyway…
options.why: A list of reasons invites bargaining: each one can be argued with. A short decision is enough.

direct.say: The renovation can wait, the relatives can wait. No excuses.

evasive.say: But all that can be sorted out… maybe after all?

options.text: You always do this: you ask at the last minute!
options.why: The generalisation “always” sounds like an accusation and triggers defensiveness. Better to talk about this specific request.

direct.say: Don’t nitpick. It happens to everyone.

evasive.say: Why like that… I didn’t do it on purpose.

options.text: OK, but this is the last time.
options.why: This is agreement again, with a threat for the future. You work on Saturday and build up resentment.

direct.say: Of course, the last time! Thanks.

evasive.say: Of course, of course, the last time!

tech.name: A positive “no”
tech.src: Ury, «The Power of a Positive No», 2007
tech.text: A clear “no” to the request plus respect for the person: without excuses, reproaches or long explanations.

nodes.hint: You need a short refusal without excuses. How to say it politely?

direct.say: So, have you decided? What’s there to think about, it’s a five-minute thing.

evasive.say: So? I’d do it myself, but I have no energy at all… You’re my only hope.

nodes.narr: The other person is pressing on your feelings. That’s expected: a refusal is usually not accepted the first time.
nodes.ask: How do you hold your decision?

options.text: I understand it’s unpleasant. I still can’t do Saturday.
options.why: Calmly repeating the decision in the same tone, without new arguments, is the “broken record” technique. You acknowledge feelings but don’t change your answer.

direct.say: Hm. OK. I won’t push any more.

evasive.say: Well… OK. I guess I’ll have to manage on my own somehow.

options.text: OK, sorry. I’ll do it.
options.why: Giving in after pressure convinces the other person that pressing is worth it. The decision is lost, and the resentment stays with you.

direct.say: Atta colleague. I knew we’d work it out.

evasive.say: Oh thank you! You’re really saving me.

options.text: This could have been planned in advance.
options.why: The accusation may be fair, but it closes the conversation and makes you the “bad one”. A request for help can be declined without a jab.

direct.say: That’s uncalled for. I thought we were friends.

evasive.say: Oh. I didn’t expect that from you.

options.text: Let’s remember who owes whom what.
options.why: Settling scores from the past turns the refusal into bargaining where whoever has the longer list wins. It has nothing to do with the request.

direct.say: Don’t start keeping accounts with me.

evasive.say: Oh, why count… I just asked.

tech.name: The “broken record”
tech.src: Smith, «When I Say No, I Feel Guilty», 1975
tech.text: Calmly repeat your decision in the same tone, without new excuses and without attacking.

nodes.hint: The decision has been said. What to do when they press on it?

direct.say: Seriously? After everything I’ve done for you?

evasive.say: I see. So nobody will help me…

nodes.narr: The pressure eases. The other person still has a problem.

options.text: I can help find a replacement: I’ll write in the team chat or tell you who to ask.
options.why: You solve their problem without sacrificing your boundary: helping find a replacement doesn’t cost your day off. This is attention to both sides’ interests.

direct.say: Hm… That’s useful. Let’s write in the chat.

evasive.say: Oh yes, that could work! Thanks for that at least.

options.text: I can take two hours in the evening, no more.
options.why: This is an acceptable compromise if you really want it. But be honest with yourself: such a “little piece” often eats up the day off too.

direct.say: Two hours is something. Let’s do it.

evasive.say: At least two hours… thank you.

options.text: That’s your problem, not mine.
options.why: Technically true, but this phrase closes the conversation and damages the relationship. You can help without sacrificing yourself.

direct.say: Well, thanks for the support.

evasive.say: So you’re that cold, it turns out.

options.text: You silently get up and leave.
options.why: Leaving without words leaves things unsaid and looks like resentment. You can end the conversation calmly.

direct.say: Hey, where are you going? We’re not done.

evasive.say: You’re leaving? Not even answering?

tech.name: Solve their problem without sacrificing your boundary
tech.text: Help doesn’t always mean “yes” to the request: you can offer something else that also solves the problem.

nodes.hint: What can you offer without giving up your day off?

direct.say: So what do I do now?

evasive.say: So what do I do… it’s all ruined.

nodes.narr: One last step: don’t leave the conversation hanging.

options.text: Thanks for understanding. If you write in the chat before Friday, I’ll help find a replacement.
options.why: A warm ending with a deadline restores contact and shows the relationship matters. The refusal didn’t become a quarrel.

direct.say: OK. I’ll write in the chat today.

evasive.say: OK… I’ll write, thanks.

options.text: Sorry, sorry, I feel so awkward…
options.why: Repeated apologies devalue the decision and bring the conversation back to guilt. You didn’t do anything wrong.

direct.say: Oh, fine, fine… Forget it.

evasive.say: Oh, it’s nothing, nothing…

options.text: Don’t be upset, OK?
options.why: Asking someone “not to be upset” shifts responsibility for their feelings onto them. They have the right to be disappointed and to cope with it.

direct.say: I’ll try.

evasive.say: Well… I’ll try.

options.text: OK, see you Monday.
options.why: Without an outcome the conversation dissolves. The next step will be new pressure.

direct.say: Mm-hm. Bye.

evasive.say: Well, bye…

tech.name: A warm ending: yes–no–yes
tech.src: Ury, «The Power of a Positive No», 2007
tech.text: End the refusal with a step closer: thanks, the decision, and an offer of what you can do.

nodes.hint: How to finish so the relationship doesn’t suffer?

direct.say: OK. We’ll see how it goes.

evasive.say: Well… fine. I’ll think of something.

direct.say: OK. Thanks for that at least.

evasive.say: OK. Good that there’s another option.

finale.title: Saying no without a quarrel
finale.lead: The refusal was said calmly, other help was offered, and the conversation ended kindly. Here’s what it relied on:
carry: Not answering right away if you’re being pressured.
Saying “no” briefly, without a list of reasons.
Offering what you really can, instead of sacrificing your boundary.
finale.prompt: How would your refusal sound in your real situation? Write down your version to come back to before the conversation.
